questions.q: What is the working principle of an electric fuse, and which effect of electric current does it utilize?
questions.a: The electric fuse works on the heating effect of electric current (Joule heating). When current exceeds the rated value, the heat produced (I²Rt) in the fuse wire raises its temperature to its melting point, causing it to melt and break the circuit. A wrong answer (e.g., "magnetic effect" or "chemical effect") reveals the student has not connected the fuse operation to the heating effect topic (c8_physics_ch2_6) and may be confusing it with electromagnets or electrolysis.

questions.q: Why is the fuse wire made of an alloy like tin-lead instead of copper, even though copper is a good conductor?
questions.a: Copper has a high melting point (1085°C) and low resistivity; a copper fuse wire would not melt quickly enough at safe overload currents, failing to protect the circuit. Tin-lead alloy has a low melting point (~180-250°C) and higher resistivity, so it produces enough heat (I²Rt) to melt rapidly at the designated overcurrent. A wrong answer (e.g., "copper is expensive" or "alloy is stronger") shows the student does not understand the critical role of melting point and resistivity in fuse design.

questions.q: A fuse wire has a resistance of 0.2 Ω. It is rated to melt when the heat produced reaches 10 J. If a current of 5 A flows through it, calculate the time after which the fuse will melt. (Use H = I²Rt)
questions.a: Given: R = 0.2 Ω, H = 10 J, I = 5 A. Formula: H = I²Rt → t = H / (I²R) = 10 J / (5² × 0.2) = 10 / (25 × 0.2) = 10 / 5 = 2 s. The fuse melts after 2 seconds. A wrong answer (e.g., 0.4 s or 20 s) reveals errors in squaring the current, unit handling, or algebraic rearrangement. The student may have forgotten to square the current (I²) or misapplied the formula.

questions.q: Two identical circuits are protected by fuses of different ratings: Fuse A (5 A) and Fuse B (10 A). The normal operating current in each circuit is 4 A. Suddenly, a fault causes the current to rise to 7 A in both. Which fuse will blow first, and why? What happens to the circuit with the other fuse?
questions.a: Fuse A (5 A) will blow first because the fault current (7 A) exceeds its rated value (5 A), producing enough heat (I²Rt) to melt it. Fuse B (10 A) will not blow because 7 A is below its rating; the circuit remains connected, risking overheating of wires and appliances. A wrong answer (e.g., "both blow" or "Fuse B blows first") shows the student does not grasp that a fuse rating is the maximum safe continuous current, not a fixed melting current for all conditions.

questions.q: A student replaces a blown 5 A fuse in a household lighting circuit with a piece of copper wire from a stranded cable. Evaluate this action: Is it safe? What are the likely consequences?
questions.a: This is extremely unsafe. Copper wire has a very high melting point and low resistance; it will not melt at currents that can overheat the circuit wiring (typically rated for 5-6 A). The copper "fuse" will not break the circuit during an overload, leading to overheating of insulation, fire risk, and damage to appliances. A wrong evaluation (e.g., "it works fine" or "copper is a better conductor so it's safer") reveals a dangerous misconception that any wire can act as a fuse, ignoring the critical requirement of a low melting point.

questions.q: Design a simple experiment using a battery, a variable resistor (rheostat), an ammeter, and different wires (copper, nichrome, tin-lead solder) to demonstrate the principle of a fuse. Describe the procedure and what you would observe.
questions.a: Connect the battery, ammeter, rheostat, and test wire in series. Gradually increase current by adjusting the rheostat. Observe and record the current at which each wire melts. The tin-lead solder will melt at the lowest current (demonstrating low melting point), nichrome at a higher current (high melting point), and copper may not melt at all within the battery's capability. A poor answer (e.g., "measure resistance of wires" or "connect in parallel") shows the student cannot translate the fuse principle into a testable experiment and confuses series/parallel connections.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: An electric fuse is a safety device that protects ______ circuits and appliances by melting and breaking the circuit when the current exceeds a specified safe limit, utilizing the heating effect of electric current (Joule heating).
Fill in the blank: ______ the fuse box in your home or the small glass fuse inside a plug top – notice the thin wire inside a ceramic or glass holder.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can explain why a fuse wire melts when excess current flows, why it must be connected in series with the live wire, and why its material must have a low melting point and appropriate rating for the circuit.
